Proposition 4 : Allow public funding of election campaigns
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 4 would lift the state ban on using public money to pay for candidates' campaigns, so state and local governments could create public campaign financing programs if they chose. It does not create any program itself. It sets broad rules: money meant for education, transportation or public safety can't be used, candidates must show broad support and accept spending limits, and public funds can't pay legal fees, fines or repay a candidate's own loans.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 4
What it does Lets the state, counties, general law cities and districts create public campaign financing programs. Creates no program
State cost A few hundred thousand dollars a year for the FPPC (Legislative Analyst)
City of LA's own program In place since 1993; $11.08 million in matching funds paid to 2026 City candidates as of Sept. 30
Vote needed Simple majority
Money raised, Jan. 1 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $756,541.89 (one committee). Against: no committee
Outside spending Against: $55,363.68, mostly Reform California's (shared with other props). For: $43,211.14
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 45% yes, 52% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 41% yes, 41% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database and the City Ethics Commission.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , What would change , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 4 mean?
State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
What does a no vote on Proposition 4 mean?
State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
What would Proposition 4 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state costs of a few hundred thousand dollars a year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public financing programs. The cost of any actual program would depend on which governments create one and how.
What it means for the City of LA
Los Angeles already runs a public matching funds program for City candidates, allowed because the current ban does not reach charter cities. Proposition 4 would not create, fund or end that program. It would let Los Angeles County, LAUSD and other local governments create programs. Proposition 4 also writes new rules for public financing programs. Neither the Legislative Analyst nor the City has said whether those rules would bind a charter city's own elections.
The details
Official title Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Type Legislative statute amending the Political Reform Act, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SB 42, Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. The Political Reform Act is a voter-approved initiative statute; the State Constitution (Article II, Section 10) lets the Legislature amend it only by a statute "approved by the electors," and provides that such measures take effect when "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
This is not the Proposition 4 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for water, wildfire and climate projects, which passed with 59.8% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 4 passes
Public money for campaigns Banned for state offices and most local offices. The ban does not apply to city elections in certain charter cities; the Analyst names Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland and Berkeley as current examples that fund campaigns (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)) The ban is lifted. The state and any local government may create a program, but none is created by the measure (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm))
Which money can be used Not applicable Public funds “earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety” cannot be used (text, Sec. 85300(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Who can get public money Not applicable Candidates who accept spending limits and meet “strict criteria” showing broad support in their district, such as a set number of small contributions or vouchers from residents. A law may not require more than $10 from each counted contributor, or a set number of signatures (text, Sec. 85300(b), (e)(7) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Spending limits Not applicable Programs may raise a participant’s limit, capped by a formula based on opponents’ money and outside spending (text, Sec. 85300(f) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Uses barred Not applicable No public funds for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s own loans. A candidate who takes public funds may never repay their own campaign loan from any source (text, Sec. 85300(c)-(d) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Fairness rule Not applicable Programs may not favor a party, incumbents or challengers (text, Sec. 85300(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who runs local programs Not applicable Each local government. The state FPPC is not responsible for running or enforcing them, but would answer questions (text, Sec. 85300(h) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm))
Illegal foreign money Fine equal to the amount contributed or spent Fine of up to three times that amount (text, Sec. 85320(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Later changes. The Legislature could change the definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC’s role by a two-thirds vote with the Governor’s signature. Changing the other rules would need another vote of the people (text, Sec. 85300(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3); Gov. Code sec. 81012 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
The City already has a program. Los Angeles voters created the City’s public matching funds program. It has been used in every City election since 1993 (City Ethics, 2019 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/news/access-to-public-matching-funds-significantly-increased-for-city-candidates/); City Ethics 2026 FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)). It is allowed today because the state ban does not apply to charter cities. The state Supreme Court ruled that in Johnson v. Bradley (1992), according to the Assembly Elections Committee’s analysis of SB 42 (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
How the City program works in 2026 (City Ethics 2026 FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)):
The City pays $6 for each $1 of a qualified contribution from an individual, up to $143 per contributor for Council and $257 for citywide offices.
To qualify, a candidate must get at least $5 each from 100 residents of the district or City, raise a minimum total from City residents ($14,300 for Council, $38,600 for City Attorney or Controller, $77,100 for Mayor), accept spending limits, cap their own money, face an opponent on the ballot, and debate or hold a town hall.
Maximum payments per candidate: $189,000 in a Council primary and $236,000 in a Council general election; $1,257,000 and $1,507,000 for Mayor.
The money comes from a City trust fund that the Charter requires the Council to fund each year, from City revenue only (City Charter sec. 471 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/wp-content/uploads/Laws-Campaigns-Matching-Funds-Charter-471.pdf)). The proposed 2026-27 budget puts $4,275,471 from the General Fund into the Matching Campaign Funds Trust Fund. The 2025-26 adopted budget shows no appropriation, after $4,075,427 in 2024-25 (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget, p. 372 (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=372)).
In the 2026 City elections , the City Ethics Commission’s totals page showed $11,076,890.66 in matching funds paid as of Sept. 30: $7,460,256.62 for the primary and $3,616,634.04 for the general election (City Ethics election totals (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)).
What Proposition 4 would and would not do to it.
Proposition 4 does not create, fund, cap or repeal the City’s program (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
It would let governments that now fall under the ban, such as Los Angeles County, LAUSD and the Community College District, create their own programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm); Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)). None would have to.
Proposition 4 rewrites the state law (Government Code Section 85300) with new conditions for any public financing program. The Legislative Analyst does not say whether those conditions would apply to a charter city’s own elections, and the Assembly committee analysis does not address it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm); Assembly Elections Committee analysis (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf)). We found no statement from the City Ethics Commission, City Attorney or City Council on Proposition 4 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
The Political Reform Act of 1974 is a voter-approved initiative statute, so the Legislature can amend it only by a two-thirds vote to further its purposes, or by a statute voters approve (Gov. Code sec. 81012 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)). SB 42 takes the second route: its text says it is submitted to the people under Article II, Section 10 of the Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Dec. 5, 2024: SB 42 was introduced. Its lead authors are Sens. Tom Umberg, Ben Allen and Cervantes; the principal coauthors include Assemblymembers Berman, Kalra, Lee and Pellerin (SB 42 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
June 2, 2025: The Senate passed it 28-10 (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
July 2, 2025: The Assembly Elections Committee approved it 5-2. Its analysis lists the California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause and League of Women Voters of California as co-sponsors, and the California Taxpayers Association as the only registered opponent (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42); Assembly Elections Committee analysis, pp. 7-9 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=7)).
Sept. 12-13, 2025: The Assembly passed it 59-20 and the Senate agreed 29-8 (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Oct. 2, 2025: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it; it became Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025 (SB 42 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. Article II, Section 10 of the State Constitution provides that the Legislature “may amend or repeal an initiative statute by another statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors,” and that an initiative statute or referendum “approved by a majority of votes cast thereon takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. II, sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)). The Political Reform Act says it may be amended “by a statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors” (Gov. Code sec. 81012(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 73 (1988) created the ban (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs); Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).
Voters rejected three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban and set up state programs: Proposition 25 (2000, 34.7% yes), Proposition 89 (2006, 25.7%) and Proposition 15 (2010, 42.7%) (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)).
City of Los Angeles: the Charter’s matching funds section was last amended by Charter Amendment H, approved March 8, 2011 (Charter sec. 471 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/wp-content/uploads/Laws-Campaigns-Matching-Funds-Charter-471.pdf)). In 2019 the Council lowered the qualifying thresholds on the Ethics Commission’s recommendation (City Ethics, July 30, 2019 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/news/access-to-public-matching-funds-significantly-increased-for-city-candidates/)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Catherine Kennedy of the California Nurses Association and Sen. Tom Umberg (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
“Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone.”
Similar systems work in “fourteen states and 26 localities.”
A local program costs “as little as $1 per resident each year.”
It “triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions.”
Their rebuttal, signed by Carmen Balber of Consumer Watchdog, Camerina Davidson of California NOW and Darius Kemp of California Common Cause, says California “is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, former FPPC commissioner Colleen McAndrews and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
There is “NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get.”
“Strict criteria” are left to “the same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money.”
Candidates could take public funds and special-interest money at the same time.
Outside the guide.
Jenny Farrell of the League of Women Voters of California told KQED that after Los Angeles adopted public financing, “14 or 15 of the members were elected using matching funds,” and the Council became majority women and people of color (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs)).
David Klein of the California Taxpayers Association told KQED that tax dollars should not go “to a candidate to then put out a hit piece mailer on an opponent” (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs)).
The Daily News editorial board wrote: “If charter cities want to keep experimenting, fine, that’s already allowed” (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).

2026 California Prop 4 guide: "Public financing" measure would let state and local governments give candidates public money for their campaigns
Proposition 4 repeals the 1988 ban that keeps the state, counties and most cities from funding campaigns. It creates no program itself; any government that wants one would set the amounts, under rules on spending limits, small-donor support and money for schools, roads and public safety.

Updated

California's Proposition 4 is asking voters whether the state and local governments may fund candidates' campaigns with public money.
Proposition 4 would repeal the California law that bars the state, counties and most cities from giving candidates public money for their campaigns, a ban voters approved in 1988.
It would not create a public financing program or spend money on any campaign. It would let the state and local governments build their own programs, under conditions written into the measure: candidates who take public funds must accept spending limits and show broad support in their district, typically through small donations, and no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety can be used. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the state's direct cost at "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions, and says the cost of any program a government chooses to create "could be significant." The measure also raises the maximum fine for illegal campaign contributions from foreign sources.
California Proposition 4 is the fourth statewide attempt to lift the 1988 public campaign financing ban, after measures in 2000, 2006 and 2010 drew between 25.7% and 42.7% yes. Prop 4, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/) placed on the ballot by SB 42, which Senator Tom Umberg wrote and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on October 2, 2025. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and one of three that change how California runs elections, alongside Proposition 5 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/california-proposition-5-2026/)'s recall changes and Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/)'s voter ID rules. California voters have turned down three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban, in 2000, 2006 and 2010, each of which also created a program; this is the first to ask only whether the ban should go. PPIC's September survey found 42% yes and 53% no, and UC Berkeley's found 35% on each side. Almost no money has been raised on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, the 1988 ban and the court fight over an earlier attempt to lift it, the cities that already fund campaigns, the cost, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 4 replaces California's ban on public campaign funds with conditions for any future program:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf) rewrites Government Code section 85300, the one-sentence ban in the Political Reform Act. Today that section says a public officer "shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, any public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office." Prop 4 keeps the prohibition only for funds "earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety," which opens every other public source to a program a government chooses to create by statute, ordinance or charter.
It then sets the ground rules. Candidates "shall abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds." The measure defines strict criteria as requirements that make candidates "demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents." A program that counts small donors cannot require any donor to give more than $10 to be counted, and it cannot require candidates to collect signatures or reach a total dollar amount above $10 per contributor. Programs may not "discriminate based on party or according to whether a candidate is a challenger or an incumbent."
Three uses of the money are banned outright. Public funds cannot pay legal defense fees or fines, and no candidate can use them to repay a personal loan to their own campaign. A candidate who takes public funds also cannot repay such a loan from any source once the campaign ends.
The measure sets no dollar amounts. It does not say how much a candidate can receive, what a match would be or how high a spending limit must be; those are left to each statute, ordinance or charter. It does cap one thing: a program may raise a participating candidate's spending limit when opponents or outside groups outspend them, but only up to a formula in the text, the highest "net supportive funds" of any other candidate in the race plus outside spending against the participating candidate, minus outside spending for them.

0 per counted contributor, signatures, or dollar totals above $10 per contributor. It leaves the specific numbers to each government (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Candidates can take public funds and special-interest money No campaign Nothing in the text bars a participating candidate from taking private contributions (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). In Los Angeles, participants may take private contributions under City limits (City Ethics FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)).
It spends no tax dollars by itself Yes campaign The Analyst says it “does not create a public campaign finance system” and that state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars a year for FPPC advice (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
As little as $1 per resident a year Yes campaign Not addressed by the Analyst. For Los Angeles, the proposed 2026-27 appropriation of $4,275,471 (City budget, p. 372 (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=372)) is about $1.10 per resident at the City’s 3,898,747 residents in the 2020 Census (LAFD report, citing the Census (https://www.fundlafire.com/s/SOC-Report.pdf)); our calculation. Matching funds actually paid in the 2026 elections were $11.08 million (City Ethics (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)).
California is the only state that bans public financing Yes campaign We did not verify this against an official source.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
On the ballot label: League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works and Consumer Watchdog (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/)).
Named in the argument in favor: California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California NOW, Californians for Disability Rights, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In and Voters Right to Know (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
Supporters of SB 42 in 2025 included the Los Angeles County Democratic Party, Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers, Fair Rep LA, Unrig LA, the Green Party of Los Angeles County, the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFSCME and ACLU California Action (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, pp. 7-9 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=7)). ACLU California Action reported spending in support in 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
On the ballot label: California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/)).
Former FPPC chair Dan Schnur and former commissioner Colleen McAndrews (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Reform California (Carl DeMaio) reported spending against it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
The legislators who voted no (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Editorial boards. The Los Angeles Daily News (Sept. 27, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)), San Diego Union-Tribune (Sept. 4, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/)) and Santa Rosa Press Democrat (Sept. 18, 2026 (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/18/pd-endorsement-no-on-prop-4-taxpayer-dollars-should-not-support-campaigns/)) editorial boards recommend a no vote. So do the Mercury News and East Bay Times: “Reject Proposition 4” (Mercury News, Oct. 19, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)). So does the San Francisco Chronicle: “We encourage you to vote no again” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 6, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026. The California State PTA voted not to take a position (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).

The City paid $11.08 million to 2026 City candidates through Sept. 30 (City Ethics election totals (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)). What happens right away. Nothing changes for voters or candidates until a government adopts a program. The FPPC would answer governments’ questions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
For Los Angeles. The City’s program continues under its Charter and ordinance. Neither the Legislative Analyst nor the City has said whether the new state conditions would apply to the City’s program; see What it means for the City .

The California Taxpayers Association raised First Amendment concerns in its 2025 opposition letter (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 6 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=6)). ### Background
***Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns.*** The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.

***Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns.*** Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.
Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
***Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs.*** Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers.
Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program.

## Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money.
Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs.
A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections.
Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.

Independent expenditures reported through Oct. 25, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Oct. 26):
Against: Reform California with Carl DeMaio reported $40,500 for slate mailers, door hangers and campaign management, with the same payments listed against other propositions. GrowSF reported $12,158.82 for digital ads and the Republican Party of San Diego County $2,704.86 for member literature.
For: the California Democratic Party ($12,220.17 for door hangers, walk pieces and mailers), ACLU California Action ($8,988.87 for its voter guide, shared), SPUR ($5,822.64, shared), Million Voter Project Action Fund ($5,299.09, shared), the ACLU Foundation of San Diego & Imperial Counties ($5,206.28, shared), Youth Power PAC ($3,815.67, shared), Community Partners ($1,040.14) and AAPI Equity Alliance ($818.28).
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Costs of any future programs “could be significant for governments that choose to create them,” depending on design (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
Assembly Elections Committee. Its analysis notes that at least seven charter cities have adopted public financing, but that programs in Richmond and Sacramento have not been funded for recent elections (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)). The Daily News reports that Oakland’s program has been postponed for fiscal reasons (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).
Los Angeles experience. The City paid $11.08 million to 2026 City candidates through Sept. 30 (City Ethics election totals (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)). We found no independent evaluation of the LA program’s effects published in 2025 or 2026.
If it passes
What happens right away. Nothing changes for voters or candidates until a government adopts a program. The FPPC would answer governments’ questions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
For Los Angeles. The City’s program continues under its Charter and ordinance. Neither the Legislative Analyst nor the City has said whether the new state conditions would apply to the City’s program; see What it means for the City .
For the County and school districts. Los Angeles County, LAUSD and other local bodies could adopt programs by statute, ordinance or charter (text, Sec. 85300 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Legal challenges. The California Taxpayers Association raised First Amendment concerns in its 2025 opposition letter (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 6 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=6)). We found no filed lawsuit as of Sept. 30, 2026.

## Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money.
Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs.
A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections.
Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.

0 per counted contributor, signatures, or dollar totals above $10 per contributor. It leaves the specific numbers to each government (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Candidates can take public funds and special-interest money No campaign Nothing in the text bars a participating candidate from taking private contributions (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). In Los Angeles, participants may take private contributions under City limits (City Ethics FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)).
It spends no tax dollars by itself Yes campaign The Analyst says it “does not create a public campaign finance system” and that state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars a year for FPPC advice (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
As little as $1 per resident a year Yes campaign Not addressed by the Analyst. For Los Angeles, the proposed 2026-27 appropriation of $4,275,471 (City budget, p. 372 (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=372)) is about $1.10 per resident at the City’s 3,898,747 residents in the 2020 Census (LAFD report, citing the Census (https://www.fundlafire.com/s/SOC-Report.pdf)); our calculation. Matching funds actually paid in the 2026 elections were $11.08 million (City Ethics (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)).
California is the only state that bans public financing Yes campaign We did not verify this against an official source.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
On the ballot label: League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works and Consumer Watchdog (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/)).
Named in the argument in favor: California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California NOW, Californians for Disability Rights, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In and Voters Right to Know (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
Supporters of SB 42 in 2025 included the Los Angeles County Democratic Party, Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers, Fair Rep LA, Unrig LA, the Green Party of Los Angeles County, the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFSCME and ACLU California Action (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, pp. 7-9 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=7)). ACLU California Action reported spending in support in 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
On the ballot label: California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/)).
Former FPPC chair Dan Schnur and former commissioner Colleen McAndrews (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Reform California (Carl DeMaio) reported spending against it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
The legislators who voted no (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Editorial boards. The Los Angeles Daily News (Sept. 27, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)), San Diego Union-Tribune (Sept. 4, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/)) and Santa Rosa Press Democrat (Sept. 18, 2026 (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/18/pd-endorsement-no-on-prop-4-taxpayer-dollars-should-not-support-campaigns/)) editorial boards recommend a no vote. So do the Mercury News and East Bay Times: “Reject Proposition 4” (Mercury News, Oct. 19, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)). So does the San Francisco Chronicle: “We encourage you to vote no again” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 6, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026. The California State PTA voted not to take a position (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).
Money for and against

The export shows two late contributions through Nov. 1: $4,500 from Sally Lieber for Board of Equalization 2026 on Oct. 27 and $2,500 from Marc Berman for Assembly 2026 on Oct. 28. The Secretary of State’s contribution totals page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-4-sb-42-umberg-political-reform-act-1974-public-campaign-financing-california-fair-elections-act-2026-ch-245-2025) still listed no committees, as of its Aug. 2 update, when checked on Sept. 30. The committee had not reached the $1 million level that triggers an FPPC top-10 list as of Oct. 17.
Who is giving
Method: every itemized contribution to committee 1488162 from Jan. 1 to Oct. 17, 2026, plus late contribution reports filed through Nov. 1, from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Nov. 2, analyzed by CityHallPass. Itemized gifts total $752,652.20; the other $3,889.69 was reported as contributions under $100 without names. Shares below are of the itemized total.
97 donors. The California Nurses Association’s PAC gave $250,000 (33.2%) on Oct. 2. With Jim Heerwagen of Los Gatos, the top two gave 46.5%.
Individuals. 82 people gave $150,669 (20.0%). Fifty-six gave $250 or less, $7,475 in all.
Out of state. The Proteus Fund (Massachusetts, $45,000), Movement Voter PAC (Massachusetts, $25,000), Common Cause (Washington, D.C., $12,192.61), the ECU Education Fund (Washington, D.C., $9,500), Stand Up America (New York, $5,000) and one individual gave $96,792.61, or 12.9%.
Political committees. The nurses’ PAC, Million More Voters (sponsored by the California Labor Federation, $100,000), the ACLU of Northern California’s election committee ($100,000), Movement Voter PAC, the California Donor Table Issues Committee ($20,000), Sen. Umberg’s ballot measure committee ($10,550), Assemblymember Alex Lee’s campaign ($10,000), Californians Defending Democracy ($7,500), Sally Lieber’s Board of Equalization campaign ($4,500) and Assemblymember Marc Berman’s campaign ($2,500).
Los Angeles. Four donors with City of Los Angeles addresses gave $1,440.59 together, including the California Clean Money Action Fund.

Where committee donors get their money. Movement Voter PAC is a federal PAC (FEC ID C00728360). Its California committee is named “Supporting Prop 4,” and its first California statement, for Sept. 22-23, 2026, reports $1,065,000 in non-California spending and $25,000 to the Yes on 4 committee (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
How the money was spent. Through Oct. 17 the committee paid David Binder Research $58,800 for polling, 50+1 Strategies $27,500 and AST Consulting $12,500 for consulting, Eldridge Political Partners $21,000, Radicle Digital $20,000 for online ads, and $10,888.17 in staff payroll and reimbursements (July-Sept. statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199944&amendid=0); Sept. 20-Oct. 17 statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215110&amendid=0)).
Outside spending
Independent expenditures reported through Oct. 25, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Oct. 26):
Against: Reform California with Carl DeMaio reported $40,500 for slate mailers, door hangers and campaign management, with the same payments listed against other propositions. GrowSF reported $12,158.82 for digital ads and the Republican Party of San Diego County $2,704.86 for member literature.
For: the California Democratic Party ($12,220.17 for door hangers, walk pieces and mailers), ACLU California Action ($8,988.87 for its voter guide, shared), SPUR ($5,822.64, shared), Million Voter Project Action Fund ($5,299.09, shared), the ACLU Foundation of San Diego & Imperial Counties ($5,206.28, shared), Youth Power PAC ($3,815.67, shared), Community Partners ($1,040.14) and AAPI Equity Alliance ($818.28).
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Costs of any future programs “could be significant for governments that choose to create them,” depending on design (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
Assembly Elections Committee. Its analysis notes that at least seven charter cities have adopted public financing, but that programs in Richmond and Sacramento have not been funded for recent elections (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)). The Daily News reports that Oakland’s program has been postponed for fiscal reasons (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).
Los Angeles experience. The City paid $11.08 million to 2026 City candidates through Sept. 30 (City Ethics election totals (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)). We found no independent evaluation of the LA program’s effects published in 2025 or 2026.
If it passes
What happens right away. Nothing changes for voters or candidates until a government adopts a program. The FPPC would answer governments’ questions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
For Los Angeles. The City’s program continues under its Charter and ordinance. Neither the Legislative Analyst nor the City has said whether the new state conditions would apply to the City’s program; see What it means for the City .
For the County and school districts. Los Angeles County, LAUSD and other local bodies could adopt programs by statute, ordinance or charter (text, Sec. 85300 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Legal challenges. The California Taxpayers Association raised First Amendment concerns in its 2025 opposition letter (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 6 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=6)). We found no filed lawsuit as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no debate focused on Proposition 4 in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Signed into law (Oct. 2, 2025) (SB 42 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Largest gift (June 25, 2026). Jim Heerwagen gave the Yes committee $100,000 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

81012.
This title may be amended or repealed by the procedures set forth in this section. If any portion of subdivision (a) is declared invalid, then subdivision (b) shall be the exclusive means of amending or repealing this title.
(a) This title may be amended to further its purposes by statute, passed in each house by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring and signed by the Governor, if at least 8 days before passage in each house, or at least 12 days before passage in each house if the previous form of the bill did not amend this title, the bill in its final form has been printed, distributed to the Members of the Legislature, and published on the internet.
(b) This title may be amended or repealed by a statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

The search pages I found only show zero-result election-night versions, like "Zero Report" and "Precincts Reporting 0%." The San Francisco page is headed for the November 3, 2026 election with results still unposted, so today is probably Election Day itself, before any votes were counted. I can't see any actual results, so I'll tell the user that and point them to the Secretary of State's results page to check again later.

I'm going to check the movement.vote page, though it's probably just a cached page without actual results. The cityhallpass page has useful campaign finance details: the Yes side raised about $757,000, mostly from the California Nurses Association PAC and several $100,000 contributions, while the opposition has no committee but has seen roughly $55,000 in independent spending. Editorial boards are split mostly against the measure, with the Sacramento Bee in favor.

I'm going to check the Sacramento Bee's endorsement directly, since the CalMatters page lists it as a Yes, and I'll also pull the text of Government Code 81012 to confirm the two-thirds versus voter-approval requirement for amendments.

I'm checking the Sacramento Bee's endorsement and the text of Government Code 81012 to confirm the amendment requirement, and I'm also considering the Mercury News and San Diego Union-Tribune editorials for their reasoning against the measure.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

SB 42
Page 1
Date of Hearing: July 2, 2025
ASSEMBLY COMMITTEE ON ELECTIONS
Gail Pellerin, Chair
SB 42 (Umberg, et al.) – As Amended June 25, 2025
SENATE VOTE: 28-10
SUBJECT: Political Reform Act of 1974: public campaign financing: California Fair Elections
Act of 2026.
SUMMARY: Allows the state and local governments to offer public campaign financing
programs. Triples the maximum potential fine for criminal violations of the ban on campaign
contributions and expenditures by foreign entities. Makes this bill operative only upon voter
approval in November 2026. Specifically, this bill:
1) Permits a public officer or candidate to expend or accept public funds for the purpose of
seeking elective office if the following conditions are met:
a) The public funds are not earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
b) Public funding programs do not discriminate based on party, or according to whether a
candidate is a challenger or an incumbent.
c) Candidates receiving public funds abide by expenditure limits and meet criteria that
demonstrate broad-based support in the district in which they are running, as specified.
Such criteria may include a requirement to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers
from a specified number of voting-age residents.
d) Public funds are not used for legal defense fees or fines or to repay a personal loan from
the candidate to their campaign, and a candidate who receives public funds does not use
any source of funds to repay a personal loan to their campaign after the campaign ends.
2) Permits a public financing program adopted in accordance with this bill to increase the
expenditure limits for participating candidates, provided that any increased limit does not
exceed a specified amount that takes into account spending by other candidates for the same
office and independent expenditures (IEs) related to candidates for the same office.
3) Provides that the Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) is not responsible for
administering or enforcing a local agency’s system of public financing of candidates, unless
the FPPC agrees to do so.
4) Permits specified provisions of this bill related to the criteria for qualifying for public
financing and the maximum increase in expenditure limits for participating candidates to be
amended by the Legislature without voter approval in the same manner that the Political
Reform Act (PRA) generally may be amended without voter approval.
SB 42
Page 2
5) Increases the potential fine for a criminal violation of the state’s ban on campaign
contributions or expenditures by specified foreign entities from an amount equal to the
amount contributed or expended, to an amount at least equal to the amount contributed or
expended and up to three times that amount.
6) Makes various findings and declarations, including the following:
a) The increasing costs of political campaigns can force candidates to rely on large
contributions from wealthy donors and special interests.
b) Such disproportionate influence can undermine the public’s trust that public officials are
performing their duties in an impartial manner and that government is serving the needs
and responding to the wishes of all citizens equally, without regard to their wealth.
c) Citizen-funded election programs, in which qualified candidates can receive public funds
for the purpose of communicating with voters rather than relying exclusively on private
donors, are currently operative in five charter cities in California, as well as numerous
other local and state jurisdictions.
d) Citizen-funded election programs encourage competition by reducing the financial
advantages of incumbency.
e) By reducing reliance on wealthy donors and special interests, citizen-funded election
programs inhibit improper practices, protect against corruption or the appearance of
corruption, and protect the political integrity of our governmental institutions.
f) The absolute prohibition on public campaign financing allows special interests to gain
disproportionate influence and unfairly favors incumbents. An exception should be
created to permit citizen-funded election programs so that elections may be conducted
more fairly.
7) Requires the Secretary of State (SOS) to submit this bill’s provisions to the voters for
approval at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election.
8) Contains a severability clause.
EXISTING LAW:
1) Creates the FPPC, and makes it responsible for the impartial, effective administration and
implementation of the PRA. (Government Code §§83100, 83111)
2) Makes violations of the PRA subject to administrative, civil, and criminal penalties.
(Government Code §§83116, 91000-91005.5)
3) Prohibits public officers from expending, and candidates from accepting, public moneys for
the purpose of seeking elective office. (Government Code §85300)
SB 42
Page 3
4) Prohibits a foreign government or foreign principal from making, directly or through any
other person, a contribution, expenditure, or IE in connection with the qualification or
support of, or opposition to, a state or local ballot measure, or in connection with the election
of a candidate to state or local office, and prohibits a person or a committee from soliciting or
accepting such a contribution, as specified. Provides that a person who violates these
provisions is guilty of a misdemeanor and shall be fined an amount equal to the amount
contributed or expended. (Government Code §85320)
5) Permits the PRA to be amended or repealed only through one of the following procedures:
a) Amendments to the PRA that further its purposes may be enacted by statute that is passed
by a two-thirds vote in each house and signed by the Governor, if the bill in its final form
has been delivered to the FPPC for distribution by a specified number of days before
passage in each house, as specified; or,
b) The PRA may be amended or repealed by a statute that becomes effective only when
approved by the electors. (Government Code §81012)
FISCAL EFFECT: According to the Senate Appropriations Committee:
1) This bill would result in one-time 2026-27 General Fund costs to the SOS, in the range of
$738,000 to $984,000, for printing and mailing costs to place a measure on the ballot in a
statewide election. Actual costs may be higher or lower, depending on the length of required
elements and the overall size of the ballot.
2) The FPPC indicates that it would incur first-year costs of $205,000, and $198,000 annually
thereafter, to implement the provisions of the bill (General Fund). FPPC would require one
attorney position to accommodate additional workload resulting from the bill. FPPC further
notes that it could incur additional enforcement costs as a result of the bill. The amount is
unknown, but potentially significant (General Fund).
COMMENTS:
1) Purpose of the Bill: According to the author:
Currently, local jurisdictions such as counties, districts, and general law cities, do
not have the option to set up [a] public fund for campaign financing, despite the
policy’s popularity among voters, as voters in several charter cities have
overwhelmingly approved public campaign financing measures in recent years.
Unfortunately, other local governments do not have the option to enact these same
policies. In 2016, bipartisan supermajorities of the legislature passed, and
Governor Jerry Brown signed, SB 1107 (Allen), which would have removed the
ban and given local governments and the state this option. However, the courts
ruled that the question must be put before the voters. SB [42] will restore control
to local governments and the state by giving counties, districts, general law cities,
and the state the same option that charter cities currently have to enact public
financing of campaigns. If passed, this measure will be placed on the November
2026 ballot for voter approval.
SB 42
Page 4
2) Public Campaign Financing Programs and Previous Legislation: In June 1974, California
voters passed an initiative—Proposition 9—that created the FPPC and codified significant
restrictions and prohibitions on candidates, officeholders and lobbyists. That initiative is
commonly known as the PRA.
In 1988, voters approved two separate initiatives that sought to regulate campaign financing
by amending the PRA: Proposition 68 and Proposition 73. Proposition 68 proposed a system
of public funding and expenditure limits for state legislative races, and passed with 53% of
the vote. Proposition 73 prohibited public funding of campaigns and set contribution limits
for state and local elections, and passed with 58% of the vote. The California Supreme Court
subsequently ruled in Taxpayers to Limit Campaign Spending v. FPPC (1990) 51 Cal. 3d
744, that because the two measures contained conflicting comprehensive regulatory schemes
they could not be merged and only one could be implemented. As such, since Proposition 73
received more affirmative votes than Proposition 68, the Court ordered the implementation of
Proposition 73 and declared all provisions of Proposition 68 invalid.
In an effort to authorize public campaign financing programs subject to certain conditions, in
2016, the Legislature approved and Governor Brown signed SB 1107 (Allen), Chapter 837,
Statutes of 2016. SB 1107 did not create any public financing programs, but instead
authorized the creation of such programs by state or local governmental entities through
separate actions by those entities. Because SB 1107 sought to amend a provision of
Proposition 73, which itself amended and became part of the PRA, the provisions of SB 1107
were subject to rules governing legislation that seeks to amend the PRA. SB 1107 contained
legislative findings and declarations that the bill furthered the purposes of the PRA, and was
enacted in a manner that complied with various procedural requirements for bills that seek to
amend the PRA without the approval of voters.
Following the enactment of SB 1107, former-Senator Quentin Kopp (who was one of the
proponents of Proposition 73) and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association challenged the
provisions of SB 1107 related to public campaign financing programs in court, alleging that
those changes did not further the purposes of the PRA, and therefore could not be enacted
without being approved by voters. In Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. Newsom (2019) 39
Cal.App.5th 158, the Third District Court of Appeal agreed, finding that SB 1107 “directly
conflicts with a primary purpose and mandate of the [PRA], as amended by subsequent voter
initiatives, to prohibit public funding of political campaigns.” In its decision, the court
affirmed a judgment by the Sacramento County Superior Court that enjoined the FPPC from
enforcing the public financing related provisions of SB 1107.
The provisions of SB 1107 that authorized public financing programs have not been repealed
since the court’s decision in Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. Nonetheless, while those
provisions remain in statute, and appear to authorize public campaign financing programs,
the PRA as enforced by the FPPC continues to prohibit public officers from expending, and
candidates from accepting, public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office.
This bill proposes to repeal the provisions of SB 1107 that sought to authorize public
campaign financing programs, and proposes to authorize state and local governments to offer
SB 42
Page 5
public campaign financing programs, subject to certain conditions. Unlike SB 1107, this bill

###### 1. What would it do?
Proposition 4 would lift a ban that has been in California law since 1988.
Under current law, a public officer cannot spend, and a candidate cannot accept, public money for the purpose of seeking elective office.
That prohibition was written into the Political Reform Act by Proposition 73, an initiative the voters approved in June 1988.^[i]^ The result is that the state, the counties, and most cities are forbidden from using taxpayer dollars to help fund campaigns.
Fifteen states and Washington, DC, currently offer some form of statewide public financing for candidates, generally through grants or matching funds and often only for specified offices.
Proposition 4 would not itself create such a program in California or require campaigns to be fully financed; it would only allow state and local governments to establish programs later under the measure’s rules.
